source_text: Olim constitit de nominum proprietate, ei illam *, qui prior et Christum suum in homines adnuntiarit et legum transnominarit. constabit itaque et de impudentia eius, qui multos dicat uenturos in nomine ipsius, quod non sit ipsius, si non Christus et Iesus creatoris est, ad quem proprietas nominum pertinet. amplius et prohibeat eos recipi, quorum et ipse par sit, ut qui proinde in nomine uenit alieno: si non, ipsius erat a mendacio nominis praeuenire discipulos, qui per proprietatem nominis possidebat ueritatem eius. uenient denique illi dicentes: ego sum Christus: recipies eos, qui consimilem recepisti; nec hic enim in nomine suo uenit. quid nunc? quando et ipse ueniet nominum dominus, Christus et Iesus creatoris, reicies illum P et quam iniquum, quam iniustum et optimo deo indignum, ut non recipias eum in suo nomine uenientem, qui alium in nomine eius recepisti! Videamus et quae signa temporibus imponat: bella, opinor., et regnum super regnum et gentem super gentem et pestem et fames terraeque motus et formidines et prodigia de caelo, quae omnia seuero et atroci deo congruunt. haec cum adicit etiam oportere fieri, quem se praestat? destructorem an probatorem creatoris? cuius dispositiones confirmat impleri oportere, quas ut optimus tam tristes quam atroces abstulisset potius quam constituisset, si non ipsius fuissent ante haec autem persecutiones eis praedicat et passiones euenturas, in martyrium utique et in salutem. accipe praedicatum in Zacharia: dominus, inquit, omnipotens proteget eos et consument illos, et lapidabunt lapidibus fundae et bibent sanguinem illorum uelut uinum et replebunt pateras quasi altaris, et saluos eos faciet dominus illo die uelut oues, populum suum, quia lapides sancti uolutant. et ne putes haec in passiones praedicari, quae illos tot bellorum nomine ab allophylis manebant, respice ad species. nemo in praedicatione bellorum legitimis armis debellandorum lapidationem enumerat popularibus coetibus magis et inermi tumultui familiarem; nemo, tanta in bello sanguinis flumina paterarum capacitate metitur aut unius altaris cruentationi adaequat; nemo oues appellat eos, qui in bello armati et ipsi ex eadem feritate certantes cadunt, sed qui in sua proprietate atque patientia dedentes potius semetipsos quam uindicantes trucidantur. denique: quia lapides, inquit, sancti uolutant, non \'quia milites pugnant\'. lapides enim sunt et fundamenta, super quae nos aedificamur, exstructi secundum Paulum super fundamenta apostolorum, qui lapides sancti oppositi omnium offensui uolutant. et hic igitur ipse cogitari uetat, quid responderi oporteat apud tribunalia, qui et Balaae quod non cogitauerat, immo contra quam cogitauerat suggessit et Moysi causato linguae tarditatem os repromisit. et sapientiam ipsam, cui nemo resistet, per Esaiam demonstrauit: hic dicet: ego dei sum, et (hic) clamabit: in nomine Iacob, et alius inscribetur in nomine Israhelis. quid enim sapientius et incontradicibilius confessione simplici et exerta in martyris nomine, \'cum deo inualescentis\', quod est interpretatio Israhelis? nec mirum, si is cohibuit praecogitationem, qui et ipse a patre excepit pronuntiandi tempestiue sumministrationem:
pass_a_gloss: It was once established concerning the property of names, to him that one, who first and announced his Christ to men and renamed the laws. It will therefore also be established concerning the impudence of him, who says many will come in his name, which is not his, if Christ is not the Creator's, to whom the property of names pertains. Furthermore, he should prohibit those from being received, whose equal he himself is, so that he who comes in an alien name: if not, it was his to prevent his disciples from the lie of the name, who possessed the truth of it through the property of the name. They will finally come saying: I am Christ: you will receive them, who received a similar one; nor does this one come in his own name. What now? When the Lord of names himself comes, Christ and Jesus of the Creator, will you reject him? And how unjust and unworthy of the best God, not to receive him coming in his own name, who received another in his name! Let us see also what signs he imposes on the times: wars, I think, and kingdom upon kingdom and nation upon nation and pestilence and famine and earthquakes and terrors and prodigies from heaven, which all suit a severe and cruel God. Since he adds that these things must also happen, what kind of God does he present? A destroyer or an approver of the Creator? Whose dispositions he confirms must be fulfilled, which the best God would have rather removed than established, if they were not his. But he predicts these persecutions and passions to them, which will happen in martyrdom and in salvation. Receive the prophecy in Zechariah: the Lord, he says, Almighty will protect them and will consume them, and they will stone them with stones of the sling and will drink their blood like wine and will fill the bowls like an altar, and the Lord will save them on that day like sheep, his people, because the holy stones roll. And lest you think these things are predicted in the passions, which they suffered in the name of so many wars from foreigners, look at the species. No one in the prediction of wars to be fought with legitimate arms enumerates stoning to popular gatherings and unarmed tumult; no one measures the rivers of blood in the capacity of bowls or equals the bloodshed of one altar; no one calls them sheep, who fall armed in war and fighting with the same ferocity, but those who give themselves up rather than avenging themselves are slaughtered in their own property and patience. Finally: because, he says, the holy stones roll, not 'because the soldiers fight'. For the stones are also the foundations, upon which we are built, constructed according to Paul upon the foundations of the apostles, who are the holy stones opposed to every offense and roll. And here therefore he himself forbids thinking what ought to be responded to in the tribunals, who also suggested to Balaam what he had not thought, and promised a mouth to Moses, who was slow of speech. And he demonstrated wisdom itself, to which no one resists, through Isaiah: this one will say: I am God's, and this one will cry out: in the name of Jacob, and another will be inscribed in the name of Israel. What is wiser and more indisputable than a simple and sincere confession in the name of a martyr, 'cum deo inualescentis', which is the interpretation of Israel? Nor is it surprising, if he restrained premeditation, who also received from the Father the timely administration of speaking.

pass_b_english: The question of who owns the names was settled long ago: the title belongs to the one who first proclaimed his Christ to humanity and rewrote the laws. The impudence of the rival claimant is equally settled—he announces that many will come in his name, yet that name is not legitimately his unless Christ and Jesus belong to the Creator, to whom the property of names rightly pertains. He ought to bar such impostors from being received, since he himself is their equal; anyone who comes in another's name is an impostor. If that were not true, it would have been his duty to shield his disciples from the lie of the name, since they possessed the truth through the property of the name. In the end, pretenders will arrive declaring, "I am the Christ," and you will welcome them because you already welcomed a similar one; that earlier claimant did not come in his own name. So what happens when the true Lord of names appears—Christ and Jesus of the Creator? Will you reject him? How unjust and unworthy of the best God, to refuse the one who comes in his own name while you accepted another who came in that same name! (Zechariah) Let us also examine the signs he assigns to the times: wars, kingdoms rising against kingdoms, nations against nations, pestilence, famine, earthquakes, terrors, and portents from heaven—all of which suit a severe and cruel God. Since he insists these things must happen, what sort of God does he present? A destroyer or an approver of the Creator? He confirms that the Creator's dispositions must be fulfilled—dispositions the best God would have removed rather than established, if they were not originally his. Yet he predicts these coming persecutions and sufferings as the pathway to martyrdom and salvation. (Zechariah 9:15-16) Receive the prophecy in Zechariah: "The Lord Almighty will protect them, and they will consume their enemies; they will stone them with slingstones and drink their blood like wine, filling the bowls like the corners of the altar. The Lord their God will save them on that day like sheep, his people, because the holy stones roll." Do not mistake this for a prediction of wartime sufferings at the hands of foreigners. Look at the details. No forecast of legitimate warfare enumerates stoning by popular, unarmed mobs. No one measures rivers of blood by the capacity of bowls or equates the slaughter to a single altar's bloodshed. No one calls combatants "sheep" when they fall armed and fighting with equal ferocity; the term belongs to those who, in their loyalty and patience, surrender themselves rather than retaliate, and so are slaughtered. The text says explicitly: "because the holy stones roll," not "because soldiers fight." Those stones are the foundations upon which we are built, constructed, as Paul teaches, on the foundation of the apostles—holy stones that roll against every offense. (Isaiah) Therefore, the Spirit himself forbids worrying about what to answer before tribunals; he who suggested to Balaam words she had not considered—indeed, contrary to what she had considered—and who promised a mouth to Moses, who pleaded slowness of speech. He demonstrated wisdom itself, which no one can resist, through Isaiah: one will say, "I belong to God," another will cry out, "In the name of Jacob," and another will be inscribed, "In the name of Israel." What confession could be wiser or more indisputable than a simple, sincere declaration in the name of a martyr—"prevailing with God," which is the meaning of Israel? It is no surprise that he restrains premeditation, since he himself received from the Father the timely administration of speech.

review.notes: Pass B fails on agency and gender regarding the Balaam passage. The Latin 'quod non cogitauerat, immo contra quam cogitauerat suggessit' refers to the Spirit/God suggesting to Balaam (masculine) what he (Balaam) had not thought, or potentially the Spirit suggesting to the situation. Pass B translates 'quod non cogitauerat' as 'words she had not considered', introducing a feminine pronoun ('she') not present in the Latin 'cogitauerat' (which is third-person singular, but the context of Balaam is masculine). More importantly, Pass B translates 'quod non cogitauerat' as 'words she had not considered', which is an addition/interpretation not in the text. Additionally, Pass B translates 'quod non cogitauerat' as 'words she had not considered' and 'contra quam cogitauerat' as 'contrary to what she had considered', which introduces a feminine gender for the subject of thought that is not in the Latin source.
uncertainties: The gender of the subject in 'cogitauerat' is ambiguous in Latin, but Pass B's specific use of 'she' is an unsupported choice.
reasons: Pass B: 'words she had not considered, indeed, contrary to what she had considered' (referring to Balaam/the subject) introduces a feminine gender 'she' not present in the Latin 'cogitauerat' and adds 'words' to the clause 'quod non cogitauerat'.
